what_its_for: Dorzolamide is an eye drop used to lower the pressure inside your eye. It is used to treat glaucoma and a condition called ocular hypertension (high eye pressure). Lowering eye pressure helps protect your vision and prevent damage to your optic nerve.
how_to_take: Wash your hands well before using these eye drops. Tilt your head back, look up, and gently pull down your lower eyelid to create a small pocket. Hold the dropper above your eye and squeeze one drop into the pocket. Close your eye gently for 1 to 2 minutes — do not blink hard or squeeze your eye shut. Press gently on the inner corner of your eye (near your nose) for about 1 minute to stop the medicine from draining into your body. If you use more than one eye drop medicine, wait at least 5 to 10 minutes between each one. Do not touch the dropper tip to your eye, fingers, or any surface to keep it clean.
dosing: The usual dose is one drop in the affected eye(s) three times a day — for example, morning, midday, and evening. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. If your doctor combined this with another eye drop (such as timolol), follow the specific directions on that label.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, use it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not use two drops at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store dorzolamide eye drops at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed when not in use. Protect it from light. Do not freeze. Keep out of reach of children. Discard the bottle as directed by your pharmacist after opening.
what_to_avoid: Do not wear soft contact lenses while using these eye drops — the preservative in the drops (benzalkonium chloride) can be absorbed by soft lenses and may irritate your eyes. Remove your contacts before using the drops and wait at least 15 minutes before putting them back in. Avoid touching the dropper tip to any surface to prevent contamination. Do not use if you are allergic to sulfa drugs (sulfonamides) without first talking to your doctor, as dorzolamide belongs to the same drug family.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice: severe eye pain, redness, or irritation; blurred vision or sudden vision changes; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; eyelid swelling or crusting; signs of a kidney stone such as severe back or side pain, blood in urine, or pain when urinating. Call your doctor if your eye pressure does not seem to be improving or if side effects bother you.
when_it_works: Dorzolamide starts lowering eye pressure within a couple of hours after the first dose. You may not feel any different because high eye pressure usually has no symptoms. Your eye doctor will check your eye pressure regularly to make sure the medicine is working. It is important to keep using it even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as dorzolamide may not be safe for you. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but only under the supervision of a doctor. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is usually needed, but older adults should be monitored closely. Sulfa allergy: If you have had an allergic reaction to sulfa antibiotics in the past, tell your doctor before using this medicine.
